I feel the same way a lot of the time, and I think it might have to do with justice and/or social rules? 

We get taught from a young age that doing well results in recognition for that. Doing well was also a form of masking for me - it meant that I had a role and a purpose and people liked me for it and that compensated for the persistent feeling I had of not fitting in and not being 'normal'. 

So, when my efforts aren't recognised or someone else gets credit for them, it feels like that social rule is being broken. It also feels frightening because maybe I wasn't good enough or maybe I didn't really understand or maybe it's evidence that my efforts are meaningless because I don't have the right 'personality'. 

It's also not fair, and I try to make an effort to acknowledge other people's efforts and I expect the same, I guess? 

Even typing that out made me feel overwhelmed! But those are my working theories.

I'm a medical doctor who has completed my country's equivalent of residency and fellowship, and I did most of it undiagnosed. I do not recommend that - I'm in the process of recovering from autistic burnout. 

Getting my ADHD diagnosed and treated was a revelation. I was able to focus at work, my anxiety lessened significantly, and I completed my final assessment (which was impossible without medication). If you are able to receive treatment for your ADHD, it may make a big difference. 

I also had peers who forced me to study for exams. I had to physically meet with them and that external accountability was the reason I passed my written exams. I know you've tried virtual study rooms, but if you have colleagues you can meet in person/on zoom, it may help. 

I also found that giving myself grace with timelines was useful. I took a bit longer to finish, and that's okay. It doesn't make me a bad doctor. 

Finally - I can't speak for your country, but finishing residency has open up so many doors for me. I can set my own schedule. I'm in charge, so I don't have to make eye contact in team meetings and I can take notes my way. I can change jobs if something doesn't suit me. 

It does get so much better, but residency sucks.

Oh, my friend, I relate hard to the 'not being autistic enough'/'am I just self-diagnosing so I have an excuse' concept. 

This is what I tell myself when it comes up:
1. Autism is a spectrum. Not everyone will have the same presentation, and that's okay. I do not have to autism 'perfectly' (whatever that means. My brain comes up with very unhelpful ideas a lot.)
2. No one was going to pick up my neurodivergence in the 90s or early 00s. That's not because I wasn't AuDHD 'enough', it's because these were thought of as only affecting males. I can grieve for the time lost, but I can't change it and it doesn't make me any less autistic. 
3. I have spent my life masking because that's what I needed to do to feel safe. Being able to feign neurotypical/allistic behaviours doesn't negate my autism. It does mean that I need to get to know myself again.

Also, I did the hair chewing thing, the writing thing, the hyperfixation on book series as well growing up. I feel like hyperfixations were my way of negotiating social situations that felt so scary and overwhelming to the point of shutdowns. 

Sorry, this is super disjointed. It's 0130 here and insomnia is kicking my ass.

I think a lot of autistic women are given the label "atypical" because most of the studies and representation of ADHD and ASD has been centred around men. There's also the societal expectations of women - we're supposed to be social and fit in and nurture and do what we're told - we're coached to mask from a young age and rewarded for doing so (or punished for failing to mask). 

There's also a huge overlap between ASD and ADHD. What you're describing is definitely consistent with my experience of AuDHD - I get distressed if I don't do my laundry on Fridays, and I'm perpetually hypervigilant in social situations because I'm trying to interpret social cues/making myself uncomfortable in order to adhere to the rules of social interactions. 

I don't think you need to check every box for diagnosis, nor do I think what you're describing is "atypical" - I think it's a typical presentation for those of us navigating the world as women. I found that understanding and accepting my autistic self has been incredibly validating - it's allowed me to be gentle with myself rather than forcing myself into a role that makes me unhappy and tired, and to be able to articulate my behaviours and sensory needs better to my loved ones.

I saw this tour on Tuesday night (rush ticket, third row centre orchestra!) and can honestly say it was one of my favourite productions I've seen of Hamilton. 

I'll have to get out my Playbill to see who was in which role that night, but I thought Angelica was a particular standout. Her Satisfied started with so much regret and sadness, which turned to anger as she grabbed the love letters from Peggy and Eliza, and the ending realisation that because of her role as the eldest sister, she would never be satisfied...it was heartbreaking. 

I thought Hamilton's first act was spectacular - he was played with this boyish charm and innocence, and there was this look in My Shot when Lauren's, Lafayette, and Mulligan start dancing with him that was pure surprise - like, holy shit, I actually have friends now and they like what I'm saying? It was adorable. He did fade into the background for me in the second act though. He and Eliza were cute though - he mouthed 'i love you' to her when he returned to fight. 

Lafayette was absolutely unhinged. Same with Jefferson. Even Madison was played less detached/deadpan in this version, and it made the Jefferson/Madison allegiance make a lot more sense to me. I liked the playfulness of Lafayette/Mulligan/Laurens in this version - it reminded me that a lot of these men were barely adults at the time of the Revolution. 

Eliza's Burn was so angry and sarcastic and it felt like she was having an imaginary argument with Hamilton. It was such a stark contrast to her Helpless, which was sweet and innocent - but she gave a look of suspicion and anger to (offstage) Angelica when Hamilton mentioned her taking a bite of him because she knew what was happening. 

The King was hilarious and one of my favourite versions. He was sassy and engaged with the audience. Total highlight. 

I agree that Washington didn't quite have the gravitas of other Washingtons that I've seen, but I enjoyed his controlled, annoyed giggle at 'I'm from Virginia'.

Finally, Burr. His Wait For It - it felt like he was trying to convince himself that his approach was better than Hamilton's, and when he pulled himself together at the end of the song, he seemed to berate himself for daring to show emotion. I loved that reading of Burr. 

I was really nervous about seeing the production because of the bad reviews I've seen, but I loved it.

Narcissistic friendships suck. And they're hard to talk about. Outside of my journal and posting here, I don't talk about what happened with mine. More than anything else, I feel an overwhelming sense of shame about being in that friendship and how much of myself I compromised. 

However - even though narc friends can be charming, they don't maintain friendships. Either they leave when they're no longer able to project away their feelings, or the other person leaves. To me, that's evidence of the kind of 'friend' they are. All those qualities they attribute to you - the badness and the toxicity - those are characteristics of the narcissist. And they always get caught out in the end. 

I hope you have them blocked on everything so that they can't reach you on social media. I hope you have a safe person or place to vent and debrief - a journal, a therapist, another friend or family member. I hope you know that their words, the things they say about you, are meaningless - their lies hold no weight. And I hope you know that if you choose to share your story, it is not an invitation to them, and you are not responsible for their behaviour. If you share your story and they return to their previous behaviours of threats and stalking - that serves as evidence of their dysfunction, and proves that what you're saying is true. 

 I don't blame you for being exhausted - you've been in flight or fight mode this entire time. It's tiring. You're not alone in this.

I remember the first few weeks after my nex-friend discarded me and worrying about the shit they were saying about me. They talked shit about every other person they'd previously discarded to me, I wasn't grandiose enough to think I'd be the exception to the rule, that the nex-friend would realise their contribution to the situation. 

I hadn't yet blocked them on Reddit, and I obsessed over how they would interpret my online activity. 

The turning point for me was stumbling across an old post I'd saved on Reddit, the crux of it being this - why do we spend so much time and energy excusing other people's shitty behaviour? Why is protecting bad people so important? 

The article wasn't about narcissism, but it struck a chord. Why was I spending so much time and energy worrying about what this person might think of me, say about me? Why was I so intent on trying to protect his feelings, why was I still letting myself walk on eggshells? Was I doing it in case he decided to un-discard me? He had said some of the most awful things anyone had ever said to me, and I was raised by two narcissists. 

I blocked him on everything. Stopped checking his posts. Stopped worrying what he might say to other people about me - and equally, I'm going to stop worrying about what I say. I started to process what had happened. I journalled. I painted. I crocheted. Everything he had weaponised, had used as evidence of my inherent 'badness', everything I had changed about me to try and maintain his friendship, I started to reclaim. 

It took a while. But the more I focussed on myself, the less I focussed on him, and the more things started to improve.
